summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes, bilateral below-knee amputations, and a history of recurrent multidrug-resistant urinary tract infections was admitted for hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury. She had recently completed a course of colistin, which was suspected to cause nephrotoxicity. Her potassium was elevated at 5.5 on presentation and managed with insulin and kayexalate in the emergency department. Creatinine peaked at 4.7 and stabilized at 4.4 with IV fluids. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis, supporting intrinsic kidney injury. The patient remained asymptomatic, with no signs of active infection; urine culture showed no growth. She was discharged home with instructions to follow up with nephrology, urology, and her primary care provider, advised to continue a low-potassium, low-phosphate diet, and to stop oral vancomycin. Medications were adjusted for renal function, and lisinopril was held.
